title: Compound type
body:
Array
[[Atomic type]] 

---

A type that holds **more than one value** under a single name. The opposite of an
[[Atomic type]].

| Type | Holds | Elements |
|---|---|---|
| [[Array]] | fixed number of values | all the same type |
| [[C-String]] | a `char` array ending in `'\0'` | all `char` |
| [[Structure]] | named fields | different types |
| [[Class]] | fields plus the operations on them | different types |

The ladder is worth reading in that order, because each row fixes a limitation of the one
above. An array holds many of one type; a struct holds many of *different* types and names
them; a class adds the functions and hides the fields. [[Parallel Array]]s are what you write
before you know about structs, and they are worse.

Compound values behave differently from atomic ones in exactly one way that matters: a
[[Structure]] is still copied wholesale by assignment and by [[Call by value]], but an
[[Array]] is not. An array parameter decays to a [[Pointer]], so the function can change the
caller's array. That asymmetry catches everybody once.
